stem_html:
The revival of interest in Zora Neale Hurston's fieldwork has been ______ by the very quality that once told against it. Her transcripts keep the hesitations and the jokes that her contemporaries edited out as noise, and it is that unedited surface which now makes them useful to linguists.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "driven"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "delayed", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "complicated", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "authenticated", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Once told against it” sounds negative, and the eye carries that negativity into the blank even though the sentence is about a reversal.
  • A word that fits half the sentence. Complication is plausible until the second sentence turns out to be entirely positive.
  • Substituting a nearby scholarly virtue. Authenticity and usefulness are different claims.

Why A is right The second sentence explains that the feature contemporaries rejected is exactly what makes the transcripts valuable now. The quality that once told against the work is the engine of the revival, so it drove it.

Why B is wrong Delayed reverses the time relation. The passage is about a revival that has happened, and it names the cause of that revival, not an obstacle to it.

Why C is wrong Complicated would need some difficulty in the second sentence, and there is none: it is that unedited surface which now makes them useful to linguists, an unqualified benefit.

Why D is wrong Authenticated concerns whether the transcripts are genuine, a question the passage never raises. It is the usefulness of the transcripts that is at stake, not their provenance.

stem_html:
Nakamura's proposal is elegant but ______: it explains the migration data beautifully, and it requires that the ice sheet retreated a full millennium earlier than every sediment core so far recovered allows.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "costly"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "unproven", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "obscure", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "derivative", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The mildest available criticism. “Unproven” is the reflex word for a bold hypothesis, and it understates a direct conflict with data.
  • Answering the first clause. “Elegant but” sets up a contrast; two choices contrast with elegance instead of with what follows the colon.
  • Skipping the number. A full millennium against every core is the size of the price being paid.

Why A is right The colon spells out a price: the proposal requires that the ice sheet retreated a full millennium earlier than the cores allow, so buying the elegant explanation means discarding the sediment record. Costly names a proposal that works only by giving something up, which is the trade the sentence describes.

Why B is wrong Unproven says evidence is lacking. The problem here is the opposite: evidence exists, and it contradicts the proposal, which is a stronger objection than an absence.

Why C is wrong Obscure would describe how hard the proposal is to follow, and the sentence has just called it elegant. Nothing about its clarity is in question.

Why D is wrong Derivative charges Nakamura with borrowing the idea. No earlier proposal is mentioned, and originality is not what the second half of the sentence measures.

stem_html:
Reviewers described the quartet's performance as ______. The players took the scherzo at a tempo no one in the hall had heard before, and yet the phrasing was so exactly what the score asks for that the effect was of hearing the movement plainly rather than newly.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "faithful"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "radical", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "restrained", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "idiosyncratic", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The blank is filled by the end of the sentence, not the middle. The startling tempo is the concession, not the claim.
  • “And yet” is the hinge. Everything before it is what the answer has to survive, not what it has to match.
  • Two choices for the same wrong half. Radical and idiosyncratic both answer the tempo.

Why A is right The sentence ends by saying the effect was of hearing the movement plainly rather than newly, and the phrasing was exactly what the score asks for. Whatever the tempo, the reading is being praised as true to the text.

Why B is wrong Radical answers only the first clause. The unprecedented tempo is real, and the “and yet” that follows exists to say that the performance did not end up sounding new.

Why C is wrong Restrained fits neither half: a tempo no one had heard before is not restraint, and the passage praises accuracy rather than modesty.

Why D is wrong Idiosyncratic would make the performance a personal reading, and the last clause insists on the opposite — that what came through was the score rather than the players.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2022 article about honeybee foraging.

A returning forager performs a waggle dance whose angle encodes the direction of a food source and whose duration encodes its distance. Because the dance is performed in the dark, on a vertical comb, and is watched by bees that touch rather than see it, researchers have long asked how much of the information survives the transfer. Okoye's marked-bee experiment gives an unexpected answer: recruits arrived at the correct distance far more reliably than at the correct direction, which is the reverse of what the dance's own precision would predict.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It explains a signalling system, raises a longstanding question about it, and reports a result that does not match expectations."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It describes an experiment, explains the method behind it, and identifies a flaw in the method.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It contrasts two competing accounts of the waggle dance and shows that the older account is correct.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It defines a term, gives examples of the term in use, and proposes a new definition.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Ordering the parts by prominence rather than by position. The experiment is the most striking element and it comes last.
  • Reading a surprise as a flaw. A result that contradicts a prediction is not a defect in the study.
  • Assuming a debate. Nothing in the text pits two accounts against each other.

Why A is right Three moves, in order: how the dance encodes direction and distance, the question about how much survives the transfer, and Okoye's result, which is the reverse of what the dance's own precision would predict.

Why B is wrong The experiment arrives in the last sentence, not the first, and no flaw in it is identified. The passage treats Okoye's result as sound and surprising.

Why C is wrong There is one account of the dance here, not two, and nothing older is vindicated. The only tension is between prediction and result.

Why D is wrong “Waggle dance” is explained rather than defined and redefined, and the passage gives no examples of the term being used.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from Sui Sin Far's 1912 story collection Mrs. Spring Fragrance.

Mrs. Spring Fragrance had been in America long enough to know that the American way of doing a kindness is to announce it beforehand and to require thanks after. She had also been in America long enough to know that her own way — which was to leave the thing done and say nothing — was read by her neighbours not as courtesy but as coldness. Between the two she had at last chosen a third: she announced the kindnesses she did not intend to do, and did the others in silence.

Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text as a whole?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It presents a resolution that belongs to neither of the two approaches the text has set against each other."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It reveals that the narrator disapproves of the customs described earlier in the text.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It concedes that the American approach described in the first sentence is the more effective of the two.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It explains why Mrs. Spring Fragrance's neighbours misread her behaviour.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A third option that looks like a compromise. It borrows a surface from each and belongs to neither.
  • Attributing an attitude the prose withholds. Irony in the situation is not disapproval in the narrator.
  • Answering with the previous sentence's job. The neighbours' misreading is already handled before this sentence begins.

Why A is right The first two sentences lay out two options and the cost of each. The third says she had at last chosen a third, and describes something that is neither: announcement without action, action without announcement.

Why B is wrong The narration is dry rather than disapproving, and no judgement of either custom is offered. The sentence reports a choice, not an opinion.

Why C is wrong Nothing is conceded to the American approach; she declines to adopt it. Her solution keeps its form and empties it of content.

Why D is wrong The misreading is explained in the second sentence, which is where the neighbours appear. The third sentence is about what she does next.

stem_html:
Text 1

Open-plan offices were sold on collaboration, and the evidence is now clear that they deliver the opposite. When two firms moved to open floors, face-to-face interaction fell by about seventy percent and electronic messaging rose. Removing the walls removed the privacy that made an approach feel safe.

Text 2

Wu's replication found the same drop in face-to-face contact but a different reason for it. In her sample the decline was concentrated entirely among employees whose desks had been moved more than thirty metres from their previous neighbours; those who stayed near their old teams talked as much as before, walls or no walls.

Based on the texts, how would Wu (Text 2) most likely characterize the explanation offered in the final sentence of Text 1?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "As unnecessary, because a change that accompanied the move accounts for the same decline."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "As incomplete, because it fails to explain why electronic messaging rose.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "As mistaken, because face-to-face interaction did not in fact decline in her sample.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "As confirmed, because employees who moved farther away had less privacy than those who stayed.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Same data, different cause. Two of the choices assume Wu disputes the observation rather than the explanation.
  • Distance and privacy both changed at once. The choice has to notice that one of them varies within her sample and the other does not.
  • Importing a detail from Text 1 that Text 2 never touches.

Why A is right Wu found the same drop and a different reason: the decline was concentrated entirely among employees whose desks had been moved more than thirty metres. Distance explains the result without any appeal to privacy, which leaves the privacy account with nothing left to do.

Why B is wrong Messaging is not discussed in Text 2 at all, so Wu is in no position to complain that the privacy account fails to explain it.

Why C is wrong She found the same drop in face-to-face contact. Her disagreement is about the cause, not about whether the effect happened.

Why D is wrong This gets her finding backwards. Those who stayed near their old teams talked as much as before even though they too lost their walls, which is precisely what privacy cannot explain.

stem_html:
Sleep researcher Halima Ndiaye proposed that the memory benefit of an afternoon nap comes from the nap's slow-wave stage rather than from the rest it provides, and that the benefit should therefore appear only in nappers who reach slow-wave sleep.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ndiaye's proposal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Among nappers who lay down for the same length of time, only those whose recordings showed slow-wave sleep recalled more words than the group who stayed awake."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Nappers recalled more words than participants who stayed awake, and longer naps produced larger gains than shorter ones.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Participants who reached slow-wave sleep reported feeling more rested than those who did not.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Participants who stayed awake but rested quietly in a dark room recalled as many words as nappers who reached slow-wave sleep.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A finding that supports the effect but not the mechanism. More sleep helping more is compatible with either explanation.
  • The choice that runs the other way. One option would falsify the proposal and reads as support because it mentions slow-wave sleep.
  • Measuring the wrong outcome. The claim is about recall, not about how rested anyone felt.

Why A is right The benefit should therefore appear only in nappers who reach slow-wave sleep. Holding time lying down constant removes rest as a variable, so the only thing separating the groups is whether slow-wave sleep occurred. The benefit appearing only in that group is exactly what the proposal predicts.

Why B is wrong Longer naps supply both more rest and more slow-wave sleep, so this cannot separate the two candidates. It confirms that napping helps, which was never in dispute.

Why C is wrong Feeling rested is a subjective report about rest, the very factor Ndiaye is trying to rule out, and it says nothing about how many words anyone recalled.

Why D is wrong This is evidence against the proposal. If quiet rest without sleep produces the same gain, slow-wave sleep is not what the benefit depends on.

stem_html:
In a study of a Bronze Age cemetery, Petrov argued that the graves containing imported amber belong to people who travelled, not to people who merely bought what travellers brought back. Petrov's argument rests on the claim that the amber graves should show a distinctive isotopic signature in the teeth if their occupants spent childhood elsewhere.

Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Petrov's argument?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Tooth enamel from the amber graves matched the isotopic signature of a region four hundred kilometres north, while enamel from the other graves matched the local signature."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Amber was found in a greater proportion of the richest graves than of the poorest ones.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Tooth enamel from every grave in the cemetery matched the isotopic signature of a region four hundred kilometres north.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "The amber in the graves came from a Baltic source rather than from any deposit within four hundred kilometres.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Evidence about the object instead of the person. The amber's origin is common ground.
  • The universal result that destroys the contrast. A signature shared by every grave cannot mark out any of them.
  • Wealth as a rival explanation dressed as support.

Why A is right The argument needs a distinctive isotopic signature in the teeth if their occupants spent childhood elsewhere, so the amber graves must differ from the rest in childhood origin. A foreign signature in the amber graves and a local one in the others is exactly the contrast the claim about the teeth predicts.

Why B is wrong Wealth would explain the amber as a purchase, which is the account Petrov is arguing against. Even read neutrally it says nothing about where anyone grew up.

Why C is wrong If everyone in the cemetery shows a foreign signature then travel does not distinguish the amber graves at all, and the pattern Petrov needs disappears.

Why D is wrong That the amber came a long way is agreed by both sides — it is what makes it imported. The question is whether the people moved, not whether the amber did.

stem_html:
A researcher measured how quickly four groups of participants detected a quiet tone while performing a visual task of varying difficulty. She concluded that detection slows as visual load rises, but that the slowing levels off rather than continuing to grow.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researcher's conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Detection time rose by about 60 milliseconds from no load to low load and by about the same again from low to medium, but by only about 13 milliseconds from medium to high."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Detection time was longest under high visual load and shortest under no visual load.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Detection time rose steadily across all four levels of visual load.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Detection time under medium load was more than 100 milliseconds greater than under no load.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Reading the tallest bar as the finding. The conclusion is about the spacing between bars, not about which is largest.
  • “Steadily” is the opposite of “levels off.” One choice describes the graph in a word that contradicts the conclusion.
  • A true comparison that misses the decisive interval.

Why A is right She concluded that detection slows as visual load rises, but that the slowing levels off rather than continuing to grow. The conclusion has two parts, a rise and a flattening, and only this choice reports both. The equal steps of about 60 milliseconds give the rise; the 13-millisecond step from medium to high is the levelling off.

Why B is wrong This gives the endpoints and nothing about the shape between them. A curve that flattens and a straight line both have their maximum at the right-hand end.

Why C is wrong “Steadily” asserts a constant rise, which is the claim the researcher's second clause denies. The last step is a fifth the size of the ones before it.

Why D is wrong The 118-millisecond gap is a true reading and it stops before the interval that matters. The evidence for levelling off lives entirely in the medium-to-high step.

stem_html: In her poem “Ledger,” the speaker describes an inherited house in terms that treat the building as a record of the people who left it rather than as a place to be lived in. Which quotation from a fictional poem would best illustrate this claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "“I do not sweep the stair; the third one keeps / the shape of where my grandmother stood to think.”"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "“The house is cold, and I have learned to keep / one room of it, and let the others go.”", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "“My grandmother stood on the stair to think, / and thought of nothing she would tell me of.”", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "“The deed is in a drawer I cannot reach, / and every year the paper grows more brown.”", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A quotation with the right subject and the wrong relation. The grandmother is in two choices; only one has the house holding her.
  • The literal record. A deed browning in a drawer is a document, not a house read as one.
  • Answering the half the claim excludes. Choosing which rooms to heat is living in a house.

Why A is right The stair is read as an inscription: the worn tread keeps the shape of a person who is gone, and the speaker refuses to sweep it because sweeping would erase the record. That is the building treated as a record of the people who left it rather than as a place to be lived in.

Why B is wrong This is entirely about habitation — which rooms are used and which are not. It is the half of the claim the poem is said not to be about.

Why C is wrong The grandmother appears, but the house does not record her; the lines are about what she withheld. Remove the stair and nothing in the quotation changes.

Why D is wrong A deed is a document rather than a building, so the record here is on paper. The claim is specifically about the building doing the recording.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2021 article about machine translation.

The systems that translate between the world's largest languages are trained on billions of sentence pairs. For a language with a small written record the same method is unavailable, and the standard workaround is to translate through a third language: Quechua to Spanish to English. Villalba shows that the workaround loses precisely the grammatical categories Spanish lacks — Quechua marks whether the speaker witnessed an event or was told of it, and by the time the sentence reaches English that marking is gone. The errors are therefore not random noise but a systematic subtraction, and adding more data will not remove them.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Translating through an intermediate language systematically strips out meaning that the intermediate language cannot express, so more data cannot fix it."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Machine translation systems perform poorly on languages with a small written record because they lack sufficient training data.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Quechua marks whether a speaker witnessed an event or was told of it, a distinction English does not make.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Translation between the world's largest languages has improved because billions of sentence pairs are available to train on.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Stopping at the cause of the problem. Data scarcity explains why the pivot method is used; the passage is about what the pivot method does.
  • Promoting the illustration. Evidentiality in Quechua is the sharpest detail in the text and it is there to prove something else.
  • The last sentence carries the weight. “Adding more data will not remove them” is what makes this an argument rather than a description.

Why A is right The passage names the workaround, shows what it costs, and draws the consequence: the errors are not random noise but a systematic subtraction, and adding more data will not remove them.

Why B is wrong Scarce data is the reason the workaround exists, which the passage gives in its second sentence as setup. The argument is about a defect in the workaround itself, and this choice stops before it.

Why C is wrong This is the example that demonstrates the point, offered with a dash in the middle of the third sentence. It is evidence, not the claim.

Why D is wrong This restates the first sentence, which exists only to set up the contrast with small languages in the second.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2018 article about the painter Alma Thomas.

Thomas taught art in a Washington junior high school for thirty-five years and did not hold a solo exhibition until she was sixty-eight. Accounts of her career often present the teaching as an interruption. Her notebooks argue against that reading: the colour exercises she set her students in the 1950s use the same short, repeated strokes and the same paired hues as the paintings she made after retiring, and she kept the exercises for decades.

According to the text, what do Thomas's notebooks indicate about her teaching?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It developed the visual methods she later used in her own paintings."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It prevented her from exhibiting her work until she was sixty-eight.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It was based on the paintings she made after she retired.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It was more highly regarded by her contemporaries than her paintings were.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The interruption reading is stated in order to be refuted, and it is the most quotable sentence in the passage.
  • Direction of influence. Two dates decide which came first.
  • A question about the notebooks, answered from the first sentence.

Why A is right The notebooks are introduced to argue against the interruption reading, and the evidence is that the colour exercises she set her students in the 1950s use the same short, repeated strokes and the same paired hues as her later paintings.

Why B is wrong The late first exhibition is a fact from the opening sentence, and the passage never says teaching caused it. This choice answers with the reading the notebooks are cited to overturn.

Why C is wrong The chronology runs the other way: the exercises are from the 1950s and the paintings came after she retired. Reversing it makes the evidence impossible.

Why D is wrong No contemporary's opinion of either the teaching or the paintings appears in the text.

stem_html:
Cave paintings are usually dated from charcoal in the pigment, which gives the age of the wood burned to make it. At one Iberian site the charcoal dates cluster around 24,000 years ago, while uranium-series dating of the thin calcite crust that has grown over the paintings gives a minimum age of 31,000 years. Both laboratories confirmed their results, and the crust demonstrably lies on top of the pigment. It follows that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the charcoal used in the pigment cannot have been the material that was burned to make these particular paintings."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "the uranium-series dates for the calcite crust are less reliable than the charcoal dates.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the paintings were made in at least two separate episodes thousands of years apart.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "charcoal dating should no longer be used on cave paintings.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Choosing which date to disbelieve. The passage closes that route with “both laboratories confirmed their results.”
  • The stratigraphy is the constraint. Crust on top of pigment fixes the order and no chronology of painting episodes can escape it.
  • Turning a local anomaly into a general rule.

Why A is right The crust lies on top of the pigment, so the pigment is older than 31,000 years. Charcoal that is only 24,000 years old cannot be part of something older than it, so that charcoal must have arrived by some other route.

Why B is wrong The passage rules this out: both laboratories confirmed their results. Discarding one of them is refusing the problem rather than resolving it.

Why C is wrong Two episodes would still leave 24,000-year-old charcoal underneath a 31,000-year-old crust, which the stratigraphy forbids. It solves nothing.

Why D is wrong One anomalous site cannot retire a method, and the passage offers the conflict as a puzzle about this pigment, not as a verdict on the technique.

stem_html:
Restaurants that post calorie counts beside menu items see, on average, no change in the calories their customers order. A study of one chain found the average unchanged but the variance sharply increased: after the counts went up, more customers ordered the very lightest items and more ordered the very heaviest, with fewer in the middle. Since the chain's menu and prices did not change, it can be concluded that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "an average that does not move can conceal opposite changes in different groups of customers."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "posting calorie counts causes most customers to order more calories than they otherwise would.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "customers do not read the calorie counts that restaurants post.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "restaurants should stop posting calorie counts beside menu items.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Reading one tail. The heavier orders are real and so are the lighter ones.
  • Inferring indifference from a flat average. The variance is the finding.
  • Sliding from a conclusion to a policy.

Why A is right More customers at both extremes and fewer in the middle, with the mean unchanged, is two opposite movements cancelling. The unchanged average is hiding them.

Why B is wrong More customers ordered the very heaviest items, and just as many more ordered the very lightest. Reporting one tail and not the other turns a symmetrical result into a one-sided claim.

Why C is wrong Behaviour changed after the counts went up, which is evidence that customers did read them. An unread label could not move anyone to either extreme.

Why D is wrong The passage supports a conclusion about what averages hide, not a recommendation. Whether posting is worthwhile depends on goals the text never states.

stem_html:
The mineral was named for the Cornish village where it was first identified ______ deposit large enough to mine has ever been found anywhere else.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "; no"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ", no", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "no", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ": no", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A long first clause that ends on a place name, which makes the whole opening read as a modifier.
  • The colon that nearly works. Related is not the same as explanatory.
  • “No” can begin a clause or continue a phrase, so the word after the blank does not settle the question by itself.

Why A is right Both halves are independent clauses with no conjunction between them, so a semicolon is the mark that can join them. The second clause is a separate statement about supply, not a specification of the first.

Why B is wrong A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a splice, however closely the two ideas are related.

Why C is wrong No punctuation at all fuses the sentences and momentarily invites the reader to attach “no deposit” to “identified,” which is not the intended reading.

Why D is wrong A colon announces that what follows will spell out what came before. The second clause here adds a fact about scarcity rather than explaining the naming, so the colon promises a link the sentence does not deliver.

stem_html:
Although the treaty was signed in 1868 and ratified the following spring ______ boundary it describes was not surveyed on the ground for another twenty-two years.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", the"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "; the", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ": the", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Length disguises dependence. Two verbs and two dates in the opening clause make it feel like a sentence.
  • The subordinator is the first word. Everything else follows from it.
  • Contrast invites a strong mark. The logical contrast between the clauses tempts a semicolon that the grammar forbids.

Why A is right “Although” subordinates everything before the blank, so what precedes is an introductory dependent clause and takes a comma before the main clause begins.

Why B is wrong A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side. The clause that opens with “Although” cannot stand alone, so there is nothing for a semicolon to join.

Why C is wrong Omitting the comma leaves a long introductory clause running straight into its main clause, which Standard English punctuates.

Why D is wrong A colon must be preceded by an independent clause, and a subordinate clause cannot supply one no matter how complete it sounds.

Zaha Hadid's first built commission, a fire station for a furniture factory in Weil am Rhein ______ used for less than a decade before it was converted into a museum of chairs.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

  • A comma that arrives one word late looks like a pause and breaks a verb from its complement.

Why A is right The appositive naming the commission opened with a comma after “commission,” so it has to be closed with a comma before the sentence resumes with its verb.

Why B is wrong Without the closing comma the appositive is left open, and the sentence reads as though “Weil am Rhein” were the thing that was used for less than a decade.

Why C is wrong A semicolon would sever the subject from its own verb, and “was used for less than a decade” cannot stand as a sentence.

Why D is wrong Placing the comma after the verb separates the verb from its complement, which no rule licenses, and still leaves the appositive unclosed.

stem_html:
The committee reached the conclusion that had been obvious to the engineers for months ______ the tower could not be strengthened in place and would have to come down.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ": the"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ", the", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "; the", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "the", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two defensible marks, one right one. The semicolon is legal and the colon is accurate, and the question asks which the sentence calls for.
  • “The conclusion that” is a promise, and a colon is how a sentence keeps it.
  • The comma splice hidden by a long first clause.

Why A is right The first clause names a conclusion without saying what it was, and the second supplies it. A colon after an independent clause is the mark for exactly that kind of specification.

Why B is wrong A comma cannot join two independent clauses on its own, and the material after the blank has its own subject and two verbs.

Why C is wrong A semicolon is grammatical here but loses the relationship. It would present the two clauses as separate statements when the second is the content of the first.

Why D is wrong With no punctuation the reader attaches “the tower” to “months” and the sentence fuses.

stem_html:
Neither the two conservators who examined the panel in 1974 nor the technician who x-rayed it a decade later ______ any sign of the underdrawing that the recent infrared scan revealed.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "reports"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "report", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "have reported", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "were reporting", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Proximity, not count. Two subjects joined by neither-nor do not add up to a plural.
  • The plural noun is the loudest thing in the sentence and it is the one the rule tells you to ignore.
  • Two of the wrong choices change tense as well as number, which hides the agreement error behind a second decision.

Why A is right With “neither ... nor” the verb agrees with the nearer subject, and the nearer subject is “the technician,” which is singular.

Why B is wrong Plural agreement takes its cue from “the two conservators,” the farther of the two subjects. In a neither-nor construction that is the one the verb ignores.

Why C is wrong This is plural for the same reason and adds a present perfect the sentence has no occasion for.

Why D is wrong The past progressive describes an action in progress at some past moment, and the sentence is reporting what the historical record shows now.

stem_html:
Recorded at a single session in 1959 and never reissued in the singer's lifetime, ______

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the album has become the most sought-after record of its decade."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "collectors have made the album the most sought-after record of its decade.", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "it is the album that collectors most seek out from that decade.", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "the decade's most sought-after record is what the album has become.", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Every choice mentions the album. Only one makes it the grammatical subject.
  • “It” postponed. A cleft that names the album later still leaves the modifier attached to a pronoun.
  • The inverted choice. Reordering the clause moves a different noun into the subject slot.

Why A is right The opening participial phrase describes something recorded and never reissued, so the subject of the main clause has to be the album. Here it is.

Why B is wrong This makes “collectors” the subject, so the sentence says the collectors were recorded in 1959 and never reissued.

Why C is wrong The subject is the pronoun “it,” whose referent arrives only after the verb. A modifier cannot attach to a subject the reader has not yet been given.

Why D is wrong The subject is “the decade's most sought-after record,” a description rather than the album itself, so the phrase modifies a category instead of the recording.

stem_html:
The eruption buried the harbour under nine metres of ash; by the time the first survey party arrived in 1631, the shoreline ______ almost two kilometres seaward.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "had moved"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "has moved", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "moves", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "would move", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “By the time” fixes the sequence, and one choice puts the events in the opposite order.
  • A past perfect is not the same as a past. The eruption clause uses simple past and is a different event.
  • The future-in-the-past reads smoothly and says the wrong thing.

Why A is right Two past events again: the party arrived, and before that the shoreline shifted. “By the time” requires the earlier event in the past perfect.

Why B is wrong The present perfect connects a past event to now, but the whole sentence is set in 1631 and closed off from the present.

Why C is wrong The simple present puts a seventeenth-century change into the reader's own time and clashes with “arrived.”

Why D is wrong “Would move” places the shift after the survey party's arrival, which reverses the order “by the time” establishes.

stem_html:
Fossils of the early bird Confuciusornis are so abundant at one Chinese locality that ______ can be sorted by wing length into what appear to be distinct size classes.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the specimens"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "they", "trap": "pronoun-ambiguity"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "it", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "these", "trap": "pronoun-ambiguity"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two plural candidates in one sentence. Grammatical agreement is not enough when more than one antecedent fits.
  • A bare demonstrative. “These” without a noun points at everything and nothing.
  • The singular pronoun with a tempting antecedent. The locality is singular and is not what gets sorted.

Why A is right The sentence contains two plural nouns that could be sorted — fossils and, arguably, the birds themselves — so a noun phrase is needed to say which. “The specimens” names them.

Why B is wrong “They” could refer to the fossils or to Confuciusornis as a group, and the sentence gives nothing that decides between them.

Why C is wrong “It” is singular and has no singular antecedent available; the only candidate, the locality, cannot be sorted by wing length.

Why D is wrong “These” standing alone as a pronoun leaves the same ambiguity as “they” and reads as an incomplete determiner besides.

stem_html:
Museums have begun returning objects taken during colonial expeditions, and the returns are often described as a loss to scholarship. ______ the Benin bronzes returned to Nigeria in 2022 have been studied more intensively in their first two years there than in the preceding forty in Europe, largely because researchers who could not obtain European visas can now reach them.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "In fact,"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Similarly,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Accordingly,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Granted,", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The reported view is not the writer's. “Often described as” marks a claim the passage is about to contest.
  • A concession marker for a refutation. “Granted” is the tempting near-miss.
  • Cause where there is contradiction.

Why A is right The second sentence contradicts the description just reported and does so with a stronger case than mere denial. “In fact” is what introduces evidence that overturns the preceding claim.

Why B is wrong “Similarly” needs the two sentences to point the same way. The first reports a loss to scholarship and the second reports a gain.

Why C is wrong “Accordingly” would make the intensive study a consequence of the loss, which inverts the logic entirely.

Why D is wrong “Granted” concedes a point to the other side. The sentence it introduces is the writer's own counterevidence, not a concession.

stem_html:
The wells at the site were dug through basalt, which yields water only where it is fractured. Two of the six struck a fracture and produce reliably. ______ the other four were abandoned within a season.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The remaining"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Likewise,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "For example,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Regardless,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two and six are the whole argument. The transition has to signal a partition, not a parallel.
  • “Likewise” after a sentence of good news is easy to accept without checking that the next sentence is bad news.
  • An example of a set is not the rest of the set.

Why A is right The sentence completes a division of the six wells that the previous sentence began. Naming the rest of the set is what carries the reader from the two that worked to the four that did not.

Why B is wrong “Likewise” asserts that the two sentences report the same outcome. Two wells producing reliably and four abandoned are opposite outcomes.

Why C is wrong The four abandoned wells are not an instance of the two productive ones; they are the complement of them.

Why D is wrong “Regardless” dismisses what came before as not mattering, but the first result is exactly what makes the second one meaningful.

stem_html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Peatlands cover about 3 percent of the world's land surface.
  • They store roughly twice as much carbon as all the world's forests.
  • Drained peat releases that carbon; rewetting stops the release.
  • Ilomaki rewetted 18 drained sites in Finland and measured emissions for six years.
  • Emissions fell by an average of 74 percent within three years and stayed low.

The student wants to emphasize the speed of the result from Ilomaki's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Across 18 rewetted Finnish sites, Ilomaki found that emissions fell by an average of 74 percent within three years and stayed low for the remainder of the six-year study."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Peatlands cover about 3 percent of the world's land surface but store roughly twice as much carbon as all the world's forests.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Ilomaki rewetted 18 drained peat sites in Finland and measured their emissions over a period of six years.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Because drained peat releases carbon and rewetting stops the release, Ilomaki's 18 Finnish sites emitted less after they were rewetted.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A goal that names a dimension. Speed requires a time, and two choices give a result with no clock on it.
  • Duration is not speed. A six-year study can report a slow change.
  • The framing notes. The first two bullets are background and belong to a different goal.

Why A is right Speed is a number attached to a time, and only this choice gives both: 74 percent within three years, with the six-year window behind it to show the drop held.

Why B is wrong This is context about peatlands generally and contains nothing from Ilomaki's study, let alone anything about how quickly it worked.

Why C is wrong Method and duration without a result. The reader learns the study lasted six years and never learns what happened in them.

Why D is wrong This reports that emissions fell and gives no magnitude and no timeframe, so the one thing the student wanted to emphasize is the one thing missing.
